units.text: Family Offices

Further to the SFC’s circular dated 7 January 2020 on the licensing obligations of family offices (the “Circular”), these FAQs seek to provide additional guidance on the implications of the licensing regime under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (the “Ordinance”) to single family offices and multi-family offices.
Expand all
Collapse all
Is there a definition for “family” or “family office” under the licensing regime?
A:

No, the Ordinance does not define “family” or “family office”.  It is noteworthy that the licensing regime does not hinge on whether an entity is called a family office or whether its clients are families.  A family office operator will have more flexibility to determine its legal form and operational structure with respect to its services to be provided.
What constitutes a single family office for the purposes of the Circular?
A:

It typically refers to an arrangement (often structured through a corporate vehicle owned or controlled by the family) under which the assets, investments and long-term interests of members of a single family are managed.  The SFC has not sought to define what relationships of blood or of law would constitute family membership because the licensing obligations under the Ordinance do not hinge on whether the clients of a family office are family members or not.
Is a single family office required to be licensed under the Ordinance?
A:

The issue of whether a single family office is required to be licensed under the Ordinance is determined by reference to three key factors, at least one of which must be present in order to give rise to a licensing obligation: firstly, the services provided by the family office constitute one or more regulated activity as defined under the Ordinance; secondly, the family office is carrying on a business in the provision of such services; and thirdly, the business is carried on in Hong Kong.

In determining whether certain asset management activities amount to a regulated activity, the definition of Type 9 regulated activity contains an intra-group carve-out for a single family office where it provides such services solely to its related entities, which are defined as its wholly owned subsidiaries, its holding company which holds all its issued shares or that holding company’s other wholly owned subsidiaries.

What amounts to “carrying on a business in Hong Kong” is not defined in the Ordinance and will need to be determined by reference to the facts of each case, including whether the person is performing an occupation or a duty which requires attention; the activity involves continuity; the activity is capable of making profit; and the activity was carried out for the purpose of making profit.  A genuine single family office arrangement, established to serve the investment needs of members of a single family, which is not being run as a business (i.e. not receiving any income, other than reimbursement of operating expenses from the family) or have the pursuit of profit as its business objective, should not in the ordinary course be considered as carrying on a business from a licensing perspective.  It is also not the SFC’s intent to extend its regulatory oversight to this type of single family office setup.

If two or more single family offices co-operate together for the purposes of sharing a common administrative infrastructure in order to reduce operating overheads, would such arrangements trigger a licensing obligation?
A:

The discussion in the response to Q3 above on the types of factors required to be present in order to give rise to a licensing obligation under the Ordinance would apply equally in these circumstances.

The sharing of office premises and administrative infrastructure by two or more family offices would not of itself automatically trigger a licensing obligation for such single family offices.  However, where two or more single family offices make arrangements for the sharing of human resources involved in investment related matters, research or the investment process, this may be regarded as a multi-family office structure (see also the response to Q5 below) and, where the provision of services is carried on as a business, increases the likelihood of a licensing obligation arising.
What constitutes a multi-family office for the purposes of the Circular and is a multi-family office required to be licensed?
A:
As mentioned in the Circular, “a multi-family office by definition serves more than one high net worth family” and such arrangements are likely to be evident.

Multi-family offices are typically established and run as commercial ventures.  The issue of whether a multi-family office is required to be licensed under the Ordinance will be primarily determined by the three key factors set out in the response to Q3.
Last update: 8 Sep 2020

judgments.rationale: The inclusive disjunction correctly captures the minimum expressed by “at least one”; “and thirdly” closes the enumeration without displacing that minimum. However, the formula answers whether the minimum is met, while the issue asks whether the licensing trigger is satisfied. “Must be present in order to” states necessity and does not expressly establish sufficiency. The opening reference to determination by three factors permits a completeness inference, but does not compel it. The ordinary-course treatment of non-business single family offices and the stated regulatory intent further challenge automatic triggering by regulated activity alone. Those passages retain qualifications and do not prove an alternative cumulative test.

should not in the ordinary course be considered as carrying on a business from a licensing perspective.
It is also not the SFC’s intent to extend its regulatory oversight to this type of single family office setup.

judgments.unresolved_question: Is the stated minimum intended to supply a sufficient selected trigger, despite its necessary-condition wording and the contextual treatment of non-business arrangements?

judgments.rationale: The source supplies no separate act of selecting a factor and no factor-specific conditions attached to such a selection. “At least one of which” quantifies over the enumerated factors. “Such services” links the business factor to the previously described services, and “the business” links the territorial factor to that business. These are substantive referential dependencies, but they do not establish the proposed selector mechanism. The absence of a formalization appropriately avoids inventing executable conditions; it does not make the proposed syntactic attachment source-supported. Nor does a Boolean vocabulary itself imply that its facts are independent.

firstly, the services provided by the family office constitute one or more regulated activity as defined under the Ordinance; secondly, the family office is carrying on a business in the provision of such services; and thirdly, the business is carried on in Hong Kong.

judgments.unresolved_question: Can any supplied wording support factor selection beyond ordinary existential quantification, or should this concern be reformulated solely as shared-service and shared-business dependencies?

judgments.rationale: This reading preserves both the inclusive minimum and the necessary force of “must be present in order to.” For the requested trigger-satisfaction question, failure of every factor excludes satisfaction under this clause; presence of a factor establishes only the necessary minimum. The contextual references to ordinary-course treatment, increased likelihood, and primary determination support caution about sufficiency without identifying additional mandatory conditions or proving conjunction. Withholding a total Boolean formalization is justified on this reading. This supports a conservative textual inference, not a finding that additional requirements necessarily exist or that the competing pragmatic completeness inference is impossible.

judgments.unresolved_question: Does the introductory description intend an exhaustive trigger, and, if so, what establishes sufficiency beyond the necessary minimum?

judgments.rationale: The distinction between satisfying a necessary minimum and satisfying the requested trigger follows directly from the modal wording. The supplied facts can express the minimum but cannot determine a complete trigger on this interpretation. The surrounding guidance does not warrant silently replacing “at least one” with “all three.” This candidate is substantively equivalent to the other necessary-minimum proposal; duplication supplies no additional evidence. Its statement that positive factor values leave satisfaction unresolved is sound as a limit on inference from this clause, rather than a claim that fuller case evidence could never resolve the obligation.

The sharing of office premises and administrative infrastructure by two or more family offices would not of itself automatically trigger a licensing obligation for such single family offices.

judgments.unresolved_question: What source clarification would justify a complete trigger over these three facts, rather than only a necessary-condition constraint?

missed_readings: A contextual cumulative reading deserves explicit consideration: the linked services, business and Hong Kong language, together with the treatment of non-business arrangements, may suggest that all three factors operate together. However, conjunction is not the literal connective supplied by “at least one.” It would be a contextual completion or repair requiring further support, not an established correction of this potentially experimental text.

The necessary-minimum reading permits a partial logical constraint: trigger satisfaction implies regulated OR business OR hong_kong. This preserves the negative inference without inventing a total Boolean trigger. None of the supplied executable proposals represents that constraint.
The dependencies in “such services” and “the business” support a shared-referent reading without a selected-factor mechanism. Any evaluation must concern the same services and business throughout.

How should the stated minimum be reconciled with the qualified non-business guidance and the express regulatory intent concerning genuine single family offices?
What material is represented by the missing source dependency, and does it clarify the relationship between the FAQ, the Circular and the Ordinance?

vocabulary_concerns: The three Boolean facts describe classified factors, not the modal relation between those factors and an obligation. Their disjunction cannot establish sufficiency merely because it is executable.

The facts must share the same office, services and business. They are not established as independent; in particular, “that business is carried on in Hong Kong” may entail or presuppose the business classification.

The source treats “carrying on a business in Hong Kong” as a case-dependent composite assessment. Splitting it into business and hong_kong requires a classification convention that the supplied packet does not verify.

The business classification must retain the source’s qualified ordinary-course treatment, income and expense-reimbursement distinctions, profit considerations and case-specific factors. These cannot safely become an unconditional single-family exemption or a mechanical profit test.

The regulated input assumes applicable carve-outs have already been resolved. The quoted intra-group carve-out concerns Type 9 and specified related entities; it does not establish a blanket exclusion from every regulated activity.

An unknown legal trigger due to missing sufficiency is distinct from runtime UNKNOWN caused by missing factual inputs. Conflict handling and other runtime conventions are implementation choices, not interpretations established by this source.

The supplied FAQ refers to incorporated authority that is not reproduced. The selected predicate must remain limited to the controlled text and classified inputs; the displayed update date and source location do not establish completeness or legal authority.
